title: Maximizing Comfort with Thermostats: Humidity, radiant temperature, and smart controls
summary: This Old House’s segment describes a multi-factor approach to comfort beyond just setting a numeric thermostat. The host explains four core factors—temperature, humidity, air velocity, and mean radiant temperature—and how humidity and surface temperature affect perceived warmth or coolness. It contrasts traditional on/off thermostats with smart, connected controls that use motion sensing, geofencing, and room-level wireless sensors to better match heating with occupancy and occupancy patterns, while noting efficiency considerations and potential rebates. The discussion also covers how oversized boilers, single-zone systems, and the difference between dry winter air versus humidified air influence comfort, and why upgrading controls can yield energy savings without replacing equipment.

Air velocity and comfort in forced-air systems
Mean radiant temperature and surface effects on comfort
Traditional clock thermostats and setback strategies
Whole-house wireless sensors and zoning concepts
Utility rebates and cost considerations for upgrading controls

sections.title: Four factors of comfort
sections.description: The host identifies four factors that determine comfort: temperature, humidity, air movement, and the mean radiant temperature of surfaces surrounding the body.

sections.title: Humidity and perceived temperature
sections.description: Humidity is highlighted as a key but often overlooked component; low humidity can feel cold or dry, while higher humidity can increase comfort at the same air temperature.

sections.title: Air velocity and comfort in hot-air systems
sections.description: Air moving through ducts can evaporate moisture from skin, making occupants feel colder even if the air is warm, which may lead to raising the set temperature.

sections.title: Mean radiant temperature and surface warmth
sections.description: The idea that the perceived temperature depends on radiant heat exchange with surrounding surfaces; warmer surfaces raise comfort by increasing mean radiant temperature.

sections.title: From standard to smart thermostats
concepts: Ease of use versus legacy models
sections.description: The transition from simple on/off thermostats to smarter versions that are easier to program and often linked to a phone for remote control.

sections.title: Geofencing and occupancy-aware heating
sections.description: Smart thermostats leverage GPS on a smartphone to anticipate when you’re approaching home and begin warming up accordingly.

sections.title: Room-level sensing and wireless sensors
sections.description: Wireless sensors placed around the home can sense movement and occupancy in specific rooms to deliver comfort where you spend time.

sections.title: Economics and rebates for upgrading controls
sections.description: The host notes that upgrading to modern controls can be cost-effective, with utilities offering rebates and often lower ongoing operating costs compared with older equipment.
